title: Canon medicinae / Avicenna, trans. Gerard of Cremona (BPL 7)
shelf_note: A 13th-century two-column Latin manuscript in Gothic book hand with red marginal rubrics. It matches the catalogue (Latin Canon, MS, c.1260). The page is on skull fractures from the surgical part of the Canon. No collection is given to test against.
structure_note: The structure counts give pages_translated 0, but the book field gives 901 and this page carries a translation, so one of the instruments is wrong (E2). The counts also show 255 printed backsteps and 268 repeats over 673 'printed' numbers. On an unfoliated-looking manuscript leaf like this one, where the only head mark is a red rubricated letter, these are most likely misread or invented page numbers (furniture read as page numbers), not a scan splice. 70 pages have no OCR.

pages.layout: two columns of Gothic book hand, red-underlined rubric notes in the left margin, a red flourished letter at the head; a strip of the facing leaf with a red marginal rubric at the right edge

ocr_errors.ocr: in fustera aut puluis in fudo fy ulino
ocr_errors.image: the line 'in [fugera] cū puluillo in fundo [?] uino' appears once on the leaf
ocr_errors.problem: Dittography. Three lines are repeated in the OCR: 'datum.', 'in fustera aut puluis in fudo fy ulino' and 'et est via q iam dea. Et melz z aure'. The leaf has each line only once.

ocr_errors.image: '…incide ꝯ discoope(ri)re / donec appareat os dubi/tatum. ꝯ si accidat fluxus sanguinis iplea/tur illud cū discoopertum est puluis sicc(us)'
ocr_errors.problem: The clause 'donec appareat os dubitatum' (until the doubtful bone appears) is dropped. Next to it, the instruction to fill the wound with dry powder is reduced to garble, so the translator guessed 'it must be stopped'.

The rubric says 'experientia', so the marginal heading is mistranslated

items.quote: possibly the meninges, the membranes covering the brain
an Arabic word kept by the Latin translator; its meaning her
remedies for wounds of the head
a gum used to close wounds
that is, without stinging or corroding
the sense seems to be that broken skull bones do not knit as
possibly the brain, which medieval writers sometimes called

missing.why: 'Noble members' is a technical term in Galenic and Avicennan medicine for the principal organs (brain, heart, liver). A general reader takes it as vague praise.
'Fistula' in the medieval surgical sense (a chronic, suppurating channel) is not the modern reader's default meaning

book_verdict: The right leaf of a genuine 13th-century Latin Canon manuscript, but the OCR of this page is largely garble: lines are repeated, a clause is dropped, and nearly every line is misread. The translation rightly carries a warning and wraps most of the text in unclear tags, but much of it is conjecture, and two broken tags show in the reader text. The notes are mostly sound glosses.
